Molecular Biology and Evolution.abstract: AbstractBackgroundThere are reported associations between Janus-kinase (JAK) inhibitors and gastrointestinal perforation in rheumatoid arthritis, raising concern about their use in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).MethodsUsing OptumLabs® Data Warehouse (2016-2023), we compared gastrointestinal perforation risk among 20 790 patients with IBD initiating JAK inhibitors, tumor necrosis factor antagonists, anti-integrins, or anti-interleukins, using multinomial propensity score-based inverse probability weighting.ResultsOver a median follow-up of 15.5 months, 693 gastrointestinal perforation events occurred (overall incidence rate, 2.15/100 person-years). No significant difference in risk of gastrointestinal perforation was observed between JAK inhibitors and any comparator therapy.ConclusionsIn this claims-based analysis, we did not observe an association between JAK inhibitors and excess gastrointestinal perforation risk in patients with IBD.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Alterations in the fungal microbiota and its interactions with the bacterial microbiota are type-specific in bowel disorders.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: The gastrointestinal (GI) microbiota are altered in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) with predominant diarrhea, but the interactions between fungal and bacterial communities remain poorly understood. We analyzed stool samples from South Korean patients with Crohn's disease (CD; n = 34), ulcerative colitis (UC; n = 76), IBS (n = 93), and healthy controls (HC; n = 122) using 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene and internal transcribed spacer 1 amplicon sequencing to characterize bacterial and fungal microbiota composition. Distinct fungal and bacterial diversity patterns were observed across disease groups relative to healthy controls. Taxa-specific analyses identified increased abundance of Candida albicans and Aspergillus ruber in CD, Saccharomyces cerevisiae in UC, and Malassezia in IBS. Inter-kingdom network analysis demonstrated that A. ruber was the fungal species most strongly interconnected with bacterial taxa in CD, including bacteria associated with GI health. Further assays showed that C. albicans increased the permeability of GI epithelial monolayers, whereas co-exposure with A. ruber reduced this effect. These findings demonstrate disease-specific alterations in fungal composition and inter-kingdom interactions across GI disorders and identify A. ruber as a previously unrecognized component of the CD-associated microbiota with potential modulatory effects on epithelial barrier integrity.IMPORTANCECrohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and irritable bowel syndrome are associated with disruptions in the gastrointestinal microbiota, but most studies have focused primarily on bacteria. Here, we examined both fungal and bacterial communities in stool samples from South Korean patients with these gastrointestinal disorders. We found that specific fungal species were associated with each disease, including Candida albicans and Aspergillus ruber in Crohn's disease. We also discovered that A. ruber was correlated with gut-health-associated bacteria and reduced the harmful effects of C. albicans on intestinal epithelial barrier function. These findings highlight the importance of fungal interactions in gastrointestinal health outcomes and suggest that fungal species, such as A. ruber, may represent future therapeutic targets or probiotic candidates for these diseases.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: The mechanism of chemotherapy resistance induced by Fusobacterium nucleatum in colorectal cancer through upregulation of ATF3 expression.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum) is frequently enriched in colorectal cancer (CRC) and implicated in poor chemotherapy response, but the host factors linking infection to chemoresistance remain incompletely defined. We investigated the effect of F. nucleatum on CRC cell responses to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and irinotecan. Using the GEO RNA-sequencing data set GSE90944 of F. nucleatum-treated CRC cells, we identified F. nucleatum-responsive host genes. Bioinformatic prioritization highlighted activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) as a candidate involved in F. nucleatum-associated chemoresistance. qPCR and Western blot analyses confirmed increased ATF3 mRNA and protein levels in F. nucleatum-infected CRC cells. F. nucleatum infection attenuated the cytotoxic effects of 5-FU and irinotecan in CRC cells. In vitro functional assays showed differences between infected and uninfected cells in relative proliferation, wound closure, cell-cycle distribution, and apoptosis under chemotherapy conditions. During treatment with either 5-FU or irinotecan, ATF3 knockdown was associated with more pronounced changes in relative cell viability and apoptosis under F. nucleatum-infected conditions, whereas ATF3 rescue partially reversed these changes. Additional interaction analyses provided statistical evidence for infection-associated differences in normalized 5-FU responses, with more robust support in HCT116 cells. In a nude mouse xenograft model, F. nucleatum infection attenuated the antitumor effects of both 5-FU and irinotecan, whereas ATF3 knockdown was associated with reduced tumor burden under F. nucleatum-infected chemotherapy conditions. Together, these findings support ATF3 as a functional host factor in F. nucleatum-associated chemotherapy responses and warrant further investigation of the F. nucleatum-ATF3 axis as a potential therapeutic target in CRC. [IMPORTANCE] Chemotherapy resistance limits colorectal cancer treatment. Fusobacterium nucleatum is enriched in colorectal cancer and associated with poor treatment response, but the host factors involved remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that Fusobacterium nucleatum reduces colorectal cancer cell sensitivity to 5-fluorouracil and irinotecan and induces activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3). During treatment with 5-fluorouracil or irinotecan, ATF3 depletion produced more pronounced changes in cell viability and apoptosis under Fusobacterium nucleatum-infected conditions, whereas ATF3 rescue partially reversed these effects. In a xenograft model, ATF3 knockdown was associated with reduced tumor burden under F. nucleatum-infected chemotherapy conditions. These findings identify an inducible host factor contributing to Fusobacterium nucleatum-associated chemoresistance and provide a rationale for further investigation of this host-microbe interaction as a potential therapeutic target.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Characterization of potential probiotic Lactobacillus spp. isolated from commercially reared pigs.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Probiotic bacteria and their products have shown significant promise as alternatives to traditional antimicrobials in the pig husbandry due to their antimicrobial activity. This study describes the comprehensive characterization of potential probiotic isolates sourced from the feces of commercial pig herds. Using high-throughput screening methodologies, sequential tests were performed, and isolates were discarded following any failure to meet a test acceptance criterion, allowing the initial 81 isolates collected to be reduced to 18 probiotic candidates in five screening steps. Whole-genome sequencing of 20 isolates revealed only 6 harbored previously reported antibiotic resistance genes and provided detailed taxonomic information. However, in vitro susceptibility testing highlighted much higher levels of antibiotic resistance, with only two isolates showing no in vitro resistance, one isolate with resistance to chloramphenicol only, and all other isolates tested (n = 26) having resistance to two or more antibiotics. Moreover, in vitro inhibition assays demonstrated that supernatants from 11 isolates significantly (P ≤ 0.05) decreased growth of Escherichia coli NCTC 13441 and ATCC 25922, Salmonella Typhimurium NCTC 12023, and Salmonella Typhimurium SL1344, with much of the activity lost after pH adjustment. Attachment of E. coli and Salmonella Typhimurium to intestinal cells was also significantly reduced (P ≤ 0.05) following preincubation with probiotic isolate P-001-01. In conclusion, pig-derived lactic acid-producing bacteria are promising candidates for probiotic use. However, careful in vitro screening of antibiotic susceptibility is required as high levels of antibiotic resistance may be present without corresponding known antibiotic resistance gene presence.IMPORTANCENew, non-antibiotic options are needed to limit post-weaning diarrhea and weight loss in commercial pig herds. Probiotic supplements have shown promise in achieving this, but a greater number of candidate probiotic strains are required, and their isolation and characterization can be a costly and lengthy process. Here, we describe a rapid, high-throughput, and cost-effective workflow for the isolation and characterization of probiotic species obtained from existing healthy pig herds. Using this workflow, we isolated and characterized a large number of lactic acid-producing bacterial isolates. Many of the isolates we obtained had high phenotypic levels of antimicrobial resistance although, for many of the isolates, there was a poor correlation between phenotypic and genotypic resistance. The results presented here highlight that while many lactic acid bacteria isolates are present within the feces of pigs from commercial herds, very few of the isolates meet the stringent guidelines required for commercial probiotic isolates.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Development of an indirect ELISA for the detection of GP3 antibodies against highly pathogenic porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) causes high mortality in piglets, leading to economic losses for the pig industry. The development of rapid and accurate detection technologies facilitates disease surveillance in pig farms and evaluation of vaccine efficacy. In this study, three antigenic regions of the GP3 protein with strong reactivity to highly pathogenic (HP)-PRRSV-positive serum were identified through overlapping peptide scanning. Subsequently, two P22 virus-like particle (VLP) constructs displaying GP3 antigenic regions were successfully generated. Based on these findings, an indirect ELISA (iELISA) for detecting PRRSV GP3 antibodies was established using P22 VLP-P3 as the coating antigen. The developed iELISA showed no cross-reactivity with positive sera against common porcine viruses, such as African swine fever virus, porcine circovirus type 2, and porcine epidemic diarrhea virus, indicating high specificity. Both intra-batch and inter-batch coefficients of variation were below 8%. The established iELISA showed an overall detection rate of 97.22% (105/108) for GP3 antibodies. In addition, kinetic analysis revealed that GP3-specific antibodies were detectable as early as 7 days post-infection following the HP-PRRSV challenge. Additionally, the iELISA showed cross-reactivity with NADC30-like PRRSV strains and a 73.10% (106/145) seropositivity rate for GP3-specific antibodies in clinical PRRSV-positive serum samples. In summary, the PRRSV GP3 antibody iELISA established in this study provides an effective tool for HP-PRRSV seromonitoring and for the evaluation of GP3-based epitope vaccine efficacy against HP-PRRSV.IMPORTANCEPorcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) causes severe economic losses in the swine industry due to high piglet mortality. GP3 is a promising target for epitope-based vaccines and is associated with neutralizing antibody responses; however, quantitative tools for monitoring GP3-specific humoral immunity are lacking. This study validated three B-cell epitopes on GP3 and developed a P22 virus-like particle (VLP)-P3-based indirect ELISA (iELISA) for GP3 antibody detection. The assay demonstrated high specificity and reproducibility, achieving high concordance with the immunofluorescence assay for GP3 antibody detection. Notably, it enabled early detection of GP3 antibodies at 7 days post-infection following the highly pathogenic (HP)-PRRSV challenge and showed cross-reactivity with sera from pigs infected with NADC30-like PRRSV. This P22 VLP-P3-based iELISA offers a reliable tool for HP-PRRSV surveillance and evaluation of GP3-based vaccines.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Evolution at range margins: Moving beyond the "evolutionary paradox" of range limits.
Marginal populations are evolutionarily heterogeneous: genetic signatures of population marginality in four European conifers.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Populations at ecological or geographic range limits experience distinctive genetic processes driven by demographic constraints, adaptation to atypical environments and reduced gene flow. These marginal populations can constitute valuable genetic resources, yet, the relationship between marginality and genetic variation remains poorly understood in forest trees. We investigated this relationship in four European conifers (Pinus pinea, Pinus pinaster, Pinus sylvestris and Taxus baccata), which share main life-history traits but represent contrasting demographic histories and evolutionary strategies. Across 230 native populations, we quantified six marginality indices related to climate, geography, or demographic history, together with five SNP-based genetic indicators describing inbreeding, genetic diversity and differentiation, genetic load, and genomic offset. Using a comparative multispecies framework, we assessed the influence of marginality on genetic indicators and evaluated the consistency of patterns across species. Historical (i.e., linked to the post-glacial colonization history) and climatic marginality mainly reflected species-specific evolutionary trajectories, whereas distance from the distribution centroid was consistently associated with lower genetic diversity and higher population differentiation across species. Importantly, marginality and genetic distinctiveness only partially overlapped, indicating that range-edge populations do not form a homogeneous evolutionary category. Overall, our findings highlight the key role of demographic isolation and historical processes in shaping genetic patterns at species' range limits. They also showed that marginal populations may represent either genetically vulnerable populations or reservoirs of unique evolutionary potential. Integrating genomic information with quantitative measures of marginality can improve assessment of population vulnerability, evolutionary resilience and conservation value in forest trees.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Partial clonality and the speed of range expansion along an environmental gradient.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Reproductive mode interacts in important ways with patterns of spatial adaptation, such as expansion of species' ranges along environmental gradients. Partial clonality (both asexual/clonal and sexual reproduction) characterizes a broad range of taxa, including important species that structure many terrestrial and marine ecosystems as well as many pathogens, pests, and invasives. We explore the interplay of invasion and local adaptation under partial clonality using an individual-based model, with space modeled as a unidimensional landscape of grid cells. An environmental gradient exists along the direction of expansion, such that the optimal phenotype changes in this direction. We investigate how the fraction of clonal reproduction (${r_c}$) and the association between random components of parent and clonal offspring phenotype ($\rho $) affect the speed of range expansion. We see slower expansion as amount of clonality (${r_c}$ or $\rho $) increases, with a sharp drop at complete clonality (${r_c},\rho $ = 1), indicating that only a small amount of sexual reproduction suffices for partially clonal populations to show very similar behavior to purely sexual populations-in clear contrast to what has been observed for spatial adaptation across two distinct demes with differing phenotypic optima. Expansion lag load (fitness differences between core and leading-edge sub-populations) is greatest at intermediate environmental gradient steepness, with both gradual and very steep change decreasing this lag load. Thus, clonality may hinder invasion by partially clonal species across an environmental gradient; the reproductive assurance benefits of asexual reproduction may be a better explanation for clonal species expansion in such cases.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Mating preference evolution has sex-opposite effects on species persistence under reproductive interference.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Reproductive interference, where interspecific mating activities have negative effects on reproductive output, can impact the expansion of one species' range into that of a related competitor. Theory to date suggests that if species recognition mechanisms evolve rapidly enough, the attenuation of reproductive interference may allow range expansions to proceed (a form of evolutionary rescue). Here, we show that sex differences cause evolvability not to have a uniformly positive effect on population fitness at the range front, nor on coexistence. We allow mate choice to evolve in males, where it takes the form of a courtship bias towards conspecific females, and/or in females, where a receptivity bias favours conspecific males. The beneficial effect of rapid evolution is highly contingent on (1) the asymmetry in the evolvability of mate preference between the two species and (2) the sex that controls the outcome of mating interactions. When female preferences dictate mating outcomes, rapid evolution increases the likelihood of range expansion by the fast evolving species, the other species being outcompeted. In contrast, rapid evolution of male mate choice has a detrimental effect on persistence in the zone of potential coexistence. We also show that if both sexes evolve their preferences, the female effect tends to override the male effect, and evolvability's net effect on population fitness remains positive. Thus, while rapid evolution of traits related to reproductive interference likely aid range expansion, case by case inference requires knowledge of the mating systems in question.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: When do leading and rear edges of the range shift slower or faster than climate? Insights from a mathematical model.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Many species have spread towards cooler climates and/or went extinct at the warm margin of their range as a result of climate warming. The large diversity in observed range shifts however remains poorly understood. We here explore how evolution of the climatic niche at range margins may alter range shifts patterns. We use previously developed mathematical results to predict the velocity at which rear and leading edge move in an asexual species adapting to an environment that changes in space and time. As in previous studies, we find a critical climate change velocity beyond which the species cannot persist. We further predict the critical climate velocities, below which, the leading edge shifts faster than climate, or the species persists at its rear edge. We derive predictions along one-dimensional and two-dimensional ranges. We also examine the effect of a local disturbance on the velocity of range limits. Our simple mathematical model shows that evolution of species climatic niches at range margins can already generate a large diversity of types of range shift in a warming climate. This diversity is also observed in simulations assuming sexual reproduction or finite population sizes. The expectation of a simple climate tracking may therefore be too simplistic, underestimating the resilience capacity at the warm margins and either overestimating or underestimating the capacity for spread at the cold margin, with important consequences for management of biodiversity in a changing climate.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Adaptation to marginal habitats at the rear edge provides resilience to future warming.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Rear-edge populations are typically relicts of glacial refugia that persist in marginal habitats at the warmer edge of species distributions. Persistence likely required adapting to postglacial climate warming. The resulting climate adaptation may affect success under future climate change if adaptative strategies align with future conditions. We explored how rear-edge populations persist in their marginal climates, and whether any adaptations affect responses to expected future warming in the North American herb Campanula americana. We raised plants from 23 rear-edge and central populations in 3 common gardens spanning their natural climatic gradient. We evaluated performance across the life cycle in each garden to identify key life stages underlying climate adaptation at the rear edge. We then predicted population performance at the key stage under future climates. Local climate adaptation at the rear edge was mainly driven by whether plants were able to initiate bolting, thereby transitioning from vegetative growth to reproduction. Rear-edge populations exhibited high bolting frequency under local warm winters, while more northern populations failed to bolt in these conditions. Bolting is cued by winter cold (vernalization) in the species, but rear-edge climates provide only a few days sufficiently cold for effective vernalization. We found that rear-edge populations have adapted to these conditions by evolving reduced vernalization requirement and sensitivity. Under projected warmer winters, bolting is expected to decline at mid-latitudes, whereas rear-edge populations are predicted to maintain high bolting. Our findings highlight that adaptations that likely allowed rear-edge populations to persist under past warming may also buffer these populations against future warming.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Macroevolutionary insights into the range limits of species and lineages.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Understanding the intrinsic and extrinsic factors that determine the range limits of species is an important goal in biology. Much work has focused on understanding the range limits of populations and individual species, whereas the factors that determine the distributions of evolutionary lineages have received less attention in the range limits literature. In this review, I highlight recent macroscale insights into the range limits of flowering plant lineages, and briefly compare these to findings from other taxa. Although life on Earth has managed to adapt to practically all environments, recent methodological and analytical advances in macroevolution and biogeography show that adaptation to novel environments is relatively rare: multiple large-scale studies estimate that well over 80% of speciation events are confined within their ancestral macroclimatic environment, or biome. This high degree of phylogenetic biome conservatism reflects that Earth is crossed by various major environmental adaptive barriers, or hard range limits, which strongly constrain the ranges of both species and lineages. These adaptive barriers differ significantly in how often they are surmounted: some barriers, such as fire, are crossed relatively frequently, whereas others, such as frost or salinity, delimit species' ranges over many millions of years. Some barriers thus structure the global distribution of terrestrial lineages more stringently than oceans between landmasses. Furthermore, broad congruencies in large-scale distributions of plants, animals, and fungi tentatively suggest that these are shaped by similar processes, and/or biotic interactions. Environmental adaptive barriers therefore provide an important framework for understanding the range limits of populations, species, and lineages.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: The relationship between evolvability and plasticity under experimental warming across species' elevational ranges.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Phenotypic variation among individuals of a population arises from differences in their genetics and environment. Variaton due to genetics and the environment may be correlated if they share underlying developmental mechanisms or selection histories. We tested empirically for links between plasticity and evolvability (genetic variance expressed on a mean-scale) over elevation gradients, on which species typically encounter predictable niche limits, range limits, and limits to adaptive evolution. We exposed plants from the elevational core and range edges of three montane and three alpine Brassicaceae species to experimental warming and measured key ecological traits that are divergent over elevation. Plasticity in these traits did not vary over elevational gradients, but populations with stronger multivariate plasticity had higher multivariate evolvability. Furthermore, the directions of multivariate plasticity and genetic variance-covariance (G-) matrices were modestly aligned in montane species but not in alpine species. Similar results were found between core and upper-edge populations, though to a weaker extent. Moreover, plasticity to warming seemed mostly non-adaptive, but slightly less so in alpine species. In summary, we provide evidence that populations that show greater environmentally induced variation to a particular cue, warming, also have higher evolvability, independent of their position along the elevational gradient. Yet, misalignment of plasticity particularly with selection indicates that plasticity may constrain persistence of montane and alpine plants under ongoing climate warming.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Native-range origin predicts genomic contribution in an experimental Mimulus guttatus invasion.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Biological invasions and range expansions act as natural experiments for understanding evolutionary processes at and beyond a species' range margin. However, unlike manipulative experiments, invasions and range expansions are less genetically tractable and often involve genotypes of uncertain origin that are subject to complex evolutionary pressures. Here, we replay the earliest stages of the colonization of the widespread North American plant species Mimulus guttatus (synonym Erythranthe guttata) in the United Kingdom. We established a common garden in the invaded range using northern and southern native genotypes, allowed plants to freely mate and recruit, and quantified the genomic contribution made after five growing seasons using whole genome pooled sequencing (Pool-Seq). Despite having lower genome-wide variation, northern genotypes contributed disproportionately to the experimental population, which showed a two-fold excess of northern relative to southern ancestry, with 63%-70% northern contribution across chromosomes. The experimental population also showed extensive individual admixture, which we detected using diagnostic short sequences (k-mers) in the Pool-Seq data. Our results indicate that preadaptation of northern genotypes, despite reduced genome-wide variation, may have facilitated the successful range expansion of M. guttatus into the UK. This work also demonstrates how "invade and resequence" experiments can be used to dissect the genomic processes underlying expansion beyond a species' native range.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Failure to invest below-ground may limit the northern expansion of invasive knotweed: lessons from a two-phase transplant experiment.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: The ecological and evolutionary processes determining species distributions and range limits remain poorly understood. Ultimately, range limits depend on the species' abilities to persist under heterogeneous conditions by adaptive differentiation and phenotypic plasticity, including transgenerational effects. To investigate ecological differentiation and transgenerational effects in the clonal invasive knotweed, Reynoutria japonica, in its introduced range in Europe, we analyzed biomass production in a two-phase transplant experiment: Plants sampled along a latitudinal gradient were planted in three sites located throughout the range, and then re-transplanted among all three sites after two years. Biomass production and allocation in the second transplant phase were generally not associated with latitude of origin, and previous growth at the same site did not promote performance. We therefore found no evidence for adaptive differentiation or adaptive transgenerational effects. However, at the northern site, with a 25% shorter season, knotweed plants invested much less biomass below-ground, even though overwintering below-ground rhizomes are essential for the species' survival and spread. The pattern was further strengthened in plants that had previously grown in the northern site. We further explored limiting climate conditions in a species distribution model for the European range and found that mean annual temperature and temperature annual range are the main predictors of the European distribution of R. japonica. Taken together, our study suggests that low temperatures and associated short growing seasons may pose a limit to the broad environmental tolerance of R. japonica and restrict its northward spread by reducing below-ground biomass accumulation.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Resurrected in the field: benefits of rapid adaptation to historic drought seen mainly at the leading edge of a plant species' range.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Montane plant populations are experiencing novel conditions due to climate change. Furthermore, climate change is causing increased climate perturbations, such as the 2012-2016 drought in the western US, remarkable in its aridity, longevity, and warmer temperatures. This drought provided an opportunity to understand how montane populations respond to extreme perturbations, including at species range limits. We resurrected seeds of the endemic annual plant, Erythranthe laciniata, collected before the drought and at the height of the drought, in a common garden experiment to understand how drought influenced evolution in contemporary field conditions. The study included nine populations across the species range, including elevational-based range edges. Over 2,100 replicates were sown in three common gardens at natural populations at low, central, and high elevations. We recorded phenology and flower production to estimate lifetime fitness. This experiment took place in 2021, a year with relatively low precipitation and high temperatures. We found higher fitness in the drought generation at the high garden, as well as the evolution of faster phenology. Additionally, we detected climate adaptation at the low and high gardens. Low-elevation populations outperformed central populations at the central garden, suggesting adaptive lags and mismatch with contemporary climate change. Together, these results indicate rapid contemporary adaptation that is beneficial at the leading edge of the species range. Nevertheless, low fitness at lower elevations may foreshadow range contraction under continued climate change.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Transitions in reproductive traits accompany biome shifts in New Zealand species of the plant genus Veronica.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Evolutionary transitions between contrasting trait values likely occur in response to selection in new or changing environments, and these trait changes may be particularly large when a lineage shifts to occupy a completely new habitat or biome. Biome shifts can have major effects on the evolution of the species involved, including anagenetic changes in morphology, physiology, or life history and accelerated cladogenesis and diversification. Biome shifts can also be viewed as movements beyond a range margin. These shifts involve overcoming the physiological barriers that previously limited establishment, but potentially also subsequent evolution in other traits under the new environmental and biotic conditions. We examined how shifts between contrasting lowland and mountain biomes corresponded with evolution of a series of vegetative and reproductive traits, particularly focusing on transitions between combined and separate sexes (hermaphroditism and dioecy or gynodioecy) and between pigmented and white flowers in New Zealand's largest native angiosperm clade, Veronica sect. Hebe. We found an association between the evolution of a dimorphic sexual system and occupying the mountain biome, but sexual system transitions and biome shifts did not coincide. White and pigmented flowers were associated with mountain and lowland biomes, respectively, with coupled biome shifts and colour transitions. These associations between biomes, sexual system and flower colour states are likely driven by differences in types and activity of pollinators between biomes. Our findings illustrate how important changes in reproductive traits can accompany biome shifts, with some changes being more closely coupled to biome shifts than others.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Temperature and soil microbial community interact to alter performance across populations of a native plant.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Contemporary environments are exposing species to novel climates and altered biotic interactions, both of which influence population persistence and geographic distributions. Here, we tested the interactive effects of soil microbial communities and temperature variation on traits and fitness of Elephantopus tomentosus (Asteraceae, L.), a perennial forb native to the southeastern U.S.A. In a growth chamber experiment, we tested whether plants are locally adapted to their home soil communities and temperatures, and whether local soil microbes could mitigate stresses associated with exposure to elevated temperatures. We exposed accessions from populations in the center and northern edge of the range to a fully factorial combination of three soil communities and two temperature levels, reflecting the current average temperature vs. potential future climates (+4 °C). We inoculated pots with field soils collected from the center of the range, the range-edge, or with a sterilized control. Plants experienced a greater reduction in reproductive fitness under elevated temperatures when exposed to sterile soil than when grown in live soil. Plants in soils from the center of the range had greater fecundity at elevated temperatures than those in northern range-edge soils and had increased growth rates under both temperatures, likely due to central-range specific microbes. Additionally, accessions from northern populations exhibited a greater reduction in fecundity under elevated temperatures than those sourced from the warmer central populations. Our study revealed that plant fitness varied with both temperature and soil microbes, highlighting the importance of accounting for biotic interactions in studies of the biological evolution of climate change.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: The evolution of plasticity in drought-related traits in central and edge populations of Mimulus cardinalis.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Phenotypic plasticity can influence population persistence, range dynamics, and evolutionary potential in heterogeneous landscapes. If adaptive, plasticity may buffer populations against environmental variability, climate change, and extreme events. Yet, few studies have examined how plasticity and its evolution vary across species' ranges. This is especially important for edge populations, which are often most vulnerable to novel conditions. The Climate Variability Hypothesis postulates that greater environmental variability selects for genotypes that exhibit greater phenotypic plasticity. However, field tests of this hypothesis across species' ranges remain rare. Using scarlet monkeyflower (Mimulus cardinalis), we combined a resurrection approach with common gardens to test whether (1) central and edge populations differ in plasticity in drought-associated traits, (2) there were evolutionary shifts in plasticity following an extreme drought, and (3) plasticity was adaptive. We measured plasticity in first flower date, specific leaf area, and leaf dry matter content across 2 leading-edge, 2 range-centre, and 2 trailing-edge populations, comparing pre-drought ancestors and post-drought descendants grown in 3 gardens spanning the latitudinal range following a historic drought event. We found significant plasticity in all traits, and plasticity in the date of first flower was greatest in trailing-edge populations that have experienced greater interannual variation in precipitation. Evolutionary changes in plasticity occurred in some populations but did not consistently increase first-year fitness. The adaptive value of plasticity was trait-specific. These results show that plasticity is shaped by both spatial and temporal environmental variation and highlight the need to examine trait- and population-level responses to understand selection on plasticity at range edges.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Geographical gradients in leaky sex expression and reproductive effort in a dioecious plant are consistent with selection during range expansion.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Range expansion involves repeated dispersal and the establishment of new populations through colonization. Natural selection is therefore expected to favour traits that enhance dispersal and enable uniparental reproduction when mates are scarce. It is known that range-edge populations may evolve increased dispersal and, in hermaphroditic species, an enhanced capacity for self-fertilization. Here, we report results from a large common-garden experiment showing that males and females of the dioecious annual herb Mercurialis annua are more likely to show "leaky" or inconstant sex expression towards the recently colonized edge of its geographical distribution in Europe than those from the eastern Mediterranean Basin, from where the species expanded its range. Range-edge populations also had greater reproductive effort (RE). Leaky sex expression allows otherwise unisexual individuals of M. annua to produce progeny by self-fertilization, a trait that may have been selected to increase reproductive assurance during the range expansion. High RE likely facilitated both colonization and subsequent population establishment. Our results show that selection during range expansions may modify reproductive traits towards range margins, extending this notion to the phenomenon of leaky sex expression in dioecious species. Previous work has shown that leaky sex expression in M. annua is strongly heritable; our results now further suggest that has been enhanced by selection for reproductive assurance towards range margins and confirm, in a natural setting, that the trait is not just an expression of developmental instability during floral development or a relic of an incomplete transition to dioecy.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Mitochondrial complex I intermediate assembly factor CIA30 is involved in the senescence and sexual reproduction of Podospora anserina.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The conserved CIA30 protein is a critical assembly factor for mitochondrial respiratory complex I. While its dysfunction in eukaryotes is linked to severe respiratory defects and mitochondrial disease, its specific roles in coordinating fungal life history traits, including the balance between aging and reproduction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the function of the CIA30 ortholog in Podospora anserina. Deletion of Pacia30 resulted in a striking dual phenotype characterized by a remarkably extended lifespan and severely impaired sexual reproduction, whereas complementation largely restored both traits. The ΔPacia30 mutant survived beyond 21 days, while sexual development was arrested before ascospore formation. Mechanistically, the mutant exhibited reduced accumulation of reactive oxygen species, accompanied by elevated antioxidant enzyme activities. In addition, the lack of PaCIA30 protein altered mitochondrial respiratory chain composition and was associated with reduced cellular NADH and ATP levels, indicating substantial changes in mitochondrial energy metabolism. Proteomic analysis further revealed extensive metabolic and protein homeostasis remodeling in the mutant. Our findings therefore identify PaCIA30 as a previously unrecognized factor associated with lifespan and sexual development, highlighting mitochondrial complex I assembly as a key link between mitochondrial function, aging, and development in P. anserina. [IMPORTANCE] Mitochondrial complex I assembly factors are conserved across eukaryotes, but their impact on life-history traits, such as lifespan and sexual development, remains underexplored. This study reveals that deletion of Pacia30 markedly extends the vegetative lifespan of Podospora anserina while blocking sexual development and preventing the production of mature ascospores. The mutant exhibits reduced ROS accumulation, enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities, and differences in the abundance of proteins associated with energy metabolism, suggesting metabolic adaptation due to the loss of PaCIA30 protein. Our findings establish PaCIA30 as an important determinant of vegetative lifespan and sexual development and highlight the connection between mitochondrial function, redox homeostasis, and fungal development. This work positions P. anserina as a powerful model for dissecting how mitochondrial rewiring can promote longevity at the expense of sexual development, with broader implications for understanding mitochondrial energy reprogramming and aging across eukaryotes.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Distinct kinetics and mechanisms of microbial inactivation of enteric viruses revealed by capsid and genome integrity.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Enteric viruses are important contaminants of surface waters and a significant burden on public health. In aquatic ecosystems, the stability of these pathogens is differentially impacted by abiotic and biotic stressors, which can exert inactivating effects. Here, we investigated the fate of two enteroviruses, echovirus 11 (E11) and coxsackievirus B5 (CVB5), and one adenovirus, human adenovirus 2 (HAdV2), in lakewater and explored the mechanisms underlying their microbial inactivation. By combining infectivity assays, genome quantification, and capsid integrity analysis, we characterized virus-specific inactivation kinetics and mechanisms and examined the relationship between infectivity loss and capsid structural integrity. We observed rapid, intermediate, and negligible decay for HAdV2, E11, and CVB5, respectively, and confirmed that microbial proteases contribute to their inactivation. In addition, we revealed that the loss of capsid structural integrity drives E11 inactivation, but not HAdV2 inactivation. Genome decay did not consistently correlate with loss of infectivity, highlighting the limitations of genome-based detection for assessing the presence of infectious viruses. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms governing virus inactivation in aquatic environments and emphasize the importance of understanding viral fate when interpreting molecular detection data to assess virus-associated microbial risks.IMPORTANCEEnteric viruses are common contaminants of surface waters and pose important risks to human health. However, the stability of these viruses in water varies widely and is influenced by many environmental factors. In this study, we investigated how microbial activity causes the inactivation of three enteric viruses in lakewater. We found substantial differences in virus stability and showed that microbial enzymes that break down proteins contribute to virus inactivation. We additionally found that virus structural damage is associated with the inactivation of one virus, but not of another, and that quantification of virus genetic material does not reliably indicate levels of infectious virus particles. These findings highlight the importance of understanding how viruses behave in surface waters and can help inform approaches for monitoring viral contamination and assessing potential risks to human health.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Implementing microbial source tracking and quantitative microbial risk assessment to characterize fecal pollution and human health risks for recreators in a rural mixed-use watershed.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Fecal contamination of surface water poses significant human health risks to recreators and is often influenced by wastewater, agriculture, and wildlife. In this study, we implemented high-throughput sequencing-based microbial source tracking (MST) and quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) to characterize fecal pollution and human health risks in a rural watershed in south-central Texas, USA. Water samples were collected from four sites at 12 time points, and bacterial community composition was characterized using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Source contributions were estimated with SourceTracker2 by comparing water samples with fecal and wastewater samples. The human-specific Bacteroides marker HF183 was quantified by qPCR and used with literature-reported HF183 and pathogen concentrations in raw sewage and treated wastewater to estimate recreational health risks associated with norovirus, Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia spp., Campylobacter jejuni, Salmonella spp., and E. coli O157:H7. Escherichia coli and HF183 concentrations consistently exceeded the U.S. EPA recreational water quality criteria and recommended risk-based thresholds, with HF183 positively correlated with precipitation. SourceTracker2 indicated that treated wastewater effluent was the dominant known contributor to riverine microbial communities, followed by untreated wastewater, chicken, and cattle feces. QMRA risk estimates varied greatly depending on whether particle aggregation was considered in the norovirus dose-response model. Sensitivity analysis identified swimming ingestion volume, norovirus concentration in treated wastewater, and the norovirus morbidity ratio as key determinants of risk. These findings highlight challenges in MST in rural watersheds, variability in risk across microbial dose-response models, and the need for improved wastewater and stormwater management to mitigate microbial pollution and protect public health. [IMPORTANCE] Understanding the sources of microbial pollution in surface waters is essential for protecting public health and guiding effective watershed management. However, identifying pollution sources in rural areas with mixed agricultural, wastewater, and wildlife inputs remains challenging. This study combines next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based microbial source tracking with quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) to link specific contamination sources to human health risks in a rural watershed. By integrating microbial community profiling, source contributions, and health risk modeling, we provide a comprehensive framework to identify dominant contributors, including treated and untreated wastewater, and quantify the associated human health risks. The approach highlights how combining molecular and health risk assessment tools can reveal pollution patterns that conventional monitoring fails to capture. These findings demonstrate the value of NGS-informed monitoring for improving water quality management and mitigating health risks in rural mixed-use watersheds.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Isolation, characterization, and ecotoxicological testing of aquaculture-native bacterial antagonists against the fish pathogen Flavobacterium psychrophilum.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Intensive aquaculture is experiencing bottlenecks due to diseases caused by bacterial pathogens, such as Flavobacterium psychrophilum, the agent of Bacterial Cold-Water Disease and Rainbow Trout Fry Syndrome in salmonids. With rising antimicrobial resistance and limited vaccine efficacy, biocontrol alternatives are needed. Here, we developed an integrated screening pipeline to isolate native bacterial antagonists of F. psychrophilum from a rainbow trout recirculating aquaculture system. Combining an agar-based inhibition assay, in silico antimicrobial resistance, and virulence screening, and ecotoxicity evaluation toward Raphidocelis subcapitata and Daphnia magna, we identified three Flavobacterium-antagonizing strains with favorable preliminary safety profiles: Pseudomonas palmensis BG17, Rhodococcus qingshengii IW15, and Janthinobacterium sp. CB21. Cell-free supernatants of these isolates suppressed F. psychrophilum growth in vitro, with concentration-dependent effects for CB21 and IW15, and across the tested supernatant dilution range for BG17. Growth of antagonists in 50 μM and 200 μM FeCl3 reduced pathogen inhibition by BG17 across all supernatant concentrations. Its iron-free supernatant absorbed near 405 nm and fluoresced at 440-445 nm, while direct FeCl3 addition shifted both signals, and growth of the antagonist in extra iron reduced them. Together with an NRPS cluster of low similarity to a characterized pyoverdine biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) and a positive CAS assay, these findings are consistent with an iron-responsive fluorescent chelator in BG17. The effect of iron on the inhibition caused by IW15 supernatant differed depending on the iron concentration tested, suggesting a more complex iron-responsive phenotype rather than a simple concentration-dependent effect. Inhibition by CB21 supernatant was not significantly affected by iron under the tested conditions, and its genome did not encode a dedicated siderophore BGC. These aquaculture-native isolates inhibit F. psychrophilum in vitro through apparently distinct mechanisms and warrant further evaluation as biocontrol candidates.IMPORTANCEWorldwide production of intensively farmed salmonids in aquaculture represents a valuable source of high-quality protein but is challenged by significant losses caused by bacterial pathogens, such as Flavobacterium psychrophilum. On a global scale, outbreaks are treated with antibiotics, leading to the development of antimicrobial resistance, while farm effluents can spread resistant bacteria into surrounding freshwater ecosystems, even reaching human pathogens with clinical relevance. Safer biocontrol alternatives are necessary, and probiotics have gained interest as a promising option. Here, we describe three native bacterial strains from a rainbow trout farming environment that through apparently distinct mechanisms inhibit the tested F. psychrophilum strain in vitro. The strains were selected via combined genomic safety and ecotoxicity screening on non-target eukaryotic organisms. By integrating functional, genomic safety, and environmental criteria early in the in vitro screening process, this study advances a One Health approach to develop sustainable disease management alternatives for aquaculture.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Codonseek: reinforcement learning-based codon optimization guided by an omics-trained reward model
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractCodon optimization is widely used to enhance recombinant protein expression without altering protein sequences, but existing approaches often rely on heuristic metrics and overlook complex interactions among codon-related factors. Here, we developed Codonseek, a reinforcement learning-based codon optimization framework integrating a translation efficiency network (TEN)-derived reward function with AlphaZero-inspired Monte Carlo tree search. Trained on paired transcriptomic and proteomic data, TEN predicts sequence-associated translational potential as optimization rewards. In the non-conventional yeast Kluyveromyces marxianus, Codonseek generated synonymous sequences with higher predicted rewards than wild-type (WT), commercially optimized sequences, and sequences generated by two deep-learning baselines, without simply maximizing conventional codon usage metrics. For experimental validation, Codonseek-optimized sequences with higher predicted rewards than the commercial designs were selected. Among these, 66.7% improved expression relative to WT, with increases of up to 87.1%, while outperforming the commercial designs by up to 46.1% and two deep-learning baselines by up to 716.3%. These results support the potential of omics-guided reinforcement learning for codon optimization.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: BERTE: hierarchical classification of transposable elements via multi-scale BERT-based representations
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractTransposable elements (TEs) are major components of eukaryotic genomes and play important roles in genome evolution and regulation, yet their accurate classification remains difficult because TE categories are hierarchically organized and many sequences are highly redundant or homologous. This redundancy can inflate reported performance if closely related elements are shared across data partitions, making reliable generalization assessment a central challenge in TE classification. To address these challenges, we propose BERTE, a hierarchical TE classification framework designed for robust prediction under similarity-controlled evaluation. BERTE combines multi-scale contextual sequence representations with protein-domain evidence and performs taxonomy-consistent prediction through a hierarchical classifier. Using a large curated benchmark constructed from 13 public TE databases with similarity-aware clustered splitting, BERTE achieves strong performance among the evaluated TE-specific, general-purpose sequence-modeling, machine-learning, and homology-based methods across hierarchical and level-specific metrics and demonstrates strong generalization on multiple independent test datasets. Overall, BERTE establishes a robust and generalizable framework for hierarchical TE classification, providing a principled solution for accurate and reliable TE classification in large-scale genomic studies.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: MitoVeritas: a dual-omics-informed AI framework for eliminating NUMT-derived artifacts in low-frequency mtDNA mutation detection
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractLow-frequency mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are promising biomarkers, yet nuclear-embedded mtDNA sequences (NUMTs) cause hard-to-eliminate false positives that largely evade consensus-based error correction, including Duplex Sequencing. We present MitoVeritas, a machine-learning framework that uses paired mtDNA–mtRNA data to define training labels and can then be applied to mtDNA data alone. Because genuine mtDNA mutations retain representation in mitochondrial transcripts whereas NUMT-derived variants usually do not, we built a benchmark from 96 hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients, reserving 81 for model development and 15 as an untouched hold-out set defined before model selection. Using 30 features in an XGBoost classifier, MitoVeritas identified 184 of 190 genuine mutations (96.8% sensitivity) and 213 of 223 NUMT-derived artifacts (95.5% specificity) in the hold-out patients. In an independent ovarian cancer patient-derived xenograft cohort, sensitivity was 99.6% and specificity 98.4%; because these labels follow the same dual-omics rules, this analysis tests cohort-level transfer rather than the labeling assumptions. A PacBio HiFi-derived benchmark, in which variant origin was assigned independently of mtRNA evidence, provided orthogonal ground truth, and MitoVeritas showed the most balanced sensitivity-specificity trade-off among the pipelines evaluated. In real-world datasets, it preserved 94.3% of mutations without NUMT support while substantially reducing NUMT-contaminated calls at 0.1%–1% variant allele frequency, and performance was maintained across the fresh-tissue, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded, and cell-line datasets examined. As development used HCC samples exclusively, performance in normal tissues, other tumor types, and other sequencing workflows remains to be established. MitoVeritas is open-source and compatible with standard short-read sequencing data.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Interpretable anticancer drug response prediction in cell lines with tissue-specific gene weighting
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractAccurate prediction of anticancer drug response from molecular profiles is central to precision oncology, yet existing deep learning models typically ignore tissue-specific gene expression patterns and rely on post-hoc explanation methods, limiting both biological insight and clinical utility. Here, we propose a tissue-aware framework that integrates tissue-specific gene weighting derived via the Rank of Outlier in K-statistics algorithm with cross-attention–based multimodal learning. By reweighting gene expression according to tissue-specific patterns, this approach explicitly encodes tissue context into the prediction pipeline. On Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer benchmarks (114 215 pairs, 181 drugs, and 682 cell lines) under the pair-level transductive split, the model achieves ${R}^2$ = 0.947 (Pearson’s r = 0.977), outperforming all reproduced baselines by a wide margin ($\Delta{R}^2$ ≥ 0.132). Exploratory gene-importance analysis recovers known drug response determinants (e.g. BRAF at rank #2 of 35 830 combined genomic features for Dabrafenib; P −4). A separate six tissue control study reduced mean squared error by 21.0% relative to unweighted inputs, with improvements in all six tissues across three seeds. These results demonstrate that, under the transductive evaluation in cancer cell lines, incorporating biological structure into model design yields pharmacogenomic models that are both highly accurate and interpretable through post-hoc, drug-conditioned gene-importance rankings. Source code is freely available at https://github.com/born-june04/drug-response-prediction.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: OMIX: predicting optimal metabolic interventions with mixed modes for enhanced microbial production
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractComputational design methods have been widely applied to strain optimization in metabolic engineering. However, most existing design methods focus on a single mode of metabolic intervention, and even when mixed intervention modes are considered, they are often modeled via intervention-specific formulations. Furthermore, many of these methods rely on the growth optimality assumption and precise gene expression levels for phenotypic prediction. We propose an efficient strain design approach, termed OMIX, which supports mixed-mode metabolic interventions, including reaction knockouts as well as flux up-regulation and down-regulation, without relying on predefined reference flux distributions. Furthermore, embedded with a customized solution technique, OMIX not only efficiently predicts optimal design strategies but also mitigates potential numerical issues effectively. We apply OMIX to the metabolic model of Escherichia coli to predict optimal metabolic interventions for three biochemical products, showing that the approach identifies high-quality strategies with improved production performance. Extensive analysis further demonstrates computational advantages and robustness of OMIX.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Evaluating agentic bioinformatics through functionality, evidence, and validation
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractLarge language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews examine biological agents from complementary perspectives, including application, architecture, agentic capability, evidence grounding, and evaluation, but rarely operationalize these properties jointly for the same system–use-case trajectory. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Functionality–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and the reported rigor of use-case-specific workflow evaluation. Validation distinguishes successful execution from replayable computation, scientific assessment, and prospective empirical testing. Using FEV, we map 319 agentic or agent-adjacent system–use-case records and 35 benchmark or evaluation resources across seven bioinformatics domains. Eight publications contributed to both categories, yielding 346 unique publications. Under prespecified criteria, 167 records were classified as full-agentic and 152 as agent-adjacent. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution were documented more frequently than replayability, prospective empirical testing, and closed-loop empirical refinement. Benchmark performance, database grounding, model predictions, and retrospective biological observations provided distinct forms of evidence but did not independently establish replayability or validate the agent-controlled workflow. These findings characterize reporting within the curated evidence map rather than field-wide prevalence. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.
